outputs.L1:
# 1914

Before our dazzled eyes the phantoms flit—
Glory and honour, wrath and righteousness—
Age-old phantoms in their bloodstained dress,
Vultures whose ravening cries the world submit
To swarm about the rock where, chained apart
In agelong torment, Prometheus finds no rest
From that divine flame burning in his breast,
While vultures rend and tear the human heart.

Not yet do blessed hours on golden wings
Bring to the crucified their sure relief;
Deeper and deeper grows the ancient grief,
Blackest and most intolerable of things.
Eternal Rebel, old and blind, forlorn,
Bound fast in chains, enslaved by every one
Of the dark gods who hide the summer sun,
Yet still art thou mankind's redemption born.

Free soul of fire, break down their chains and bars,
Drive out these unclean phantoms of the brain,
Till every living thing be friends again,
And our lost earth true comrade to the stars.

---

**Note on revisions:** I preserved the sonnet's original meaning, imagery, and Prometheus/war allegory while refining word choices for greater musicality and precision (e.g., "wrath and righteousness" retained for its stark contrast; "ravening cries the world submit / To swarm" clarifies the syntax slightly while keeping the vulture imagery vivid). The closing quatrain remains largely intact, as its plea for liberation and universal fellowship was already powerfully rendered in the original. Let me know if you'd like a version that adheres more strictly to the original phrasing, or one that leans further into modernized diction.
outputs.L2:
**1914**

Before our blinded vision, specters dance—
Honor and glory, sanctimonious rage,
Ancient ghosts wrapped in blood-soaked garments,
Carrion birds whose screams devour the earth,
Circling the crag where, bound and isolated,
Through endless torment Prometheus cannot escape
The sacred fire consuming him within,
While talons rip the flesh of humankind.

No golden-winged salvation comes as yet
To ease the burden of those nailed to suffering;
The old wound only deepens with the years,
Becoming the darkest of unbearable truths.

Blind, sorrowful, forever in revolt,
Fettered still by every shadowed god
Who blocks the summer light from reaching us—
And yet you remain our only hope of rescue.

Liberated flame, shatter these restraints,
Banish the fevered visions from our minds,
Until all creatures find their kinship restored,
And this forsaken world rejoins the stars as kin.
outputs.L3:
# The Phantoms of 1914: Prometheus and the Eternal Torment of Humanity

The poem opens with a haunting vision of the world convulsed by four destructive phantoms: glory, honor, wrath, and righteousness. These abstract ideals, so often invoked to justify human conflict, are stripped of their noble veneer and reimagined as bloodstained, vulture-like forces descending upon the earth. Set against the backdrop of 1914—the fateful year marking the outbreak of the First World War—the poem suggests that the very virtues nations claim to defend are, in truth, predatory illusions that feed upon human suffering. Glory becomes a carrion bird circling the battlefield; honor and righteousness, rather than elevating humanity, participate in its slaughter. This opening image sets the tone for a meditation on how civilization's proudest ideals can mask its deepest savagery.

At the heart of the poem stands the towering figure of Prometheus, the ancient Titan condemned to eternal suffering for his defiance of the gods. Chained to his rock, he becomes the enduring symbol of humanity's own perpetual torment. The divine fire he once stole and carried in his breast—representing knowledge, enlightenment, and the spark of human progress—remains within him still, but it brings no comfort. Instead, vultures continually descend to tear at his heart, an image that mirrors the four destructive phantoms unleashed upon the world. Just as Prometheus is punished endlessly for his gift to humankind, so too does humanity seem doomed to suffer endlessly for its own aspirations toward progress and civilization.

Crucially, the poem insists that despite the vast span of centuries separating the mythic age from 1914, nothing has changed. No relief has come, no salvation has descended to ease this ancient wound. If anything, the grief has only deepened with time, accumulating weight and darkness across generations. What was once a singular, mythic punishment has become, in the poem's vision, the very pattern of human history—repeating itself with each new war, each new atrocity committed in the name of glory or righteousness. This grief, the poem suggests, is not merely one affliction among many but the darkest and most fundamental sorrow of human existence: the recognition that suffering perpetuates itself without end or purpose.

Yet the poem does not leave Prometheus as a static emblem of despair alone. He is reimagined as the "Eternal Rebel"—a figure who, though blind, aged, and enslaved by dark and indifferent gods, nevertheless retains his significance as humanity's ultimate hope for salvation. This paradoxical portrayal—weakened and diminished, yet still essential—captures the tension between despair and hope that runs throughout the poem. Prometheus's blindness suggests the loss of clear vision or guidance; his age speaks to the exhaustion of endless suffering; his enslavement to dark gods reflects humanity's continued subjugation to destructive forces beyond its control. And yet, embedded within this broken figure remains the possibility of redemption, for he alone carries the fire that could yet illuminate a better path.

The poem concludes with an impassioned plea directed at this diminished but still-vital spirit. The speaker calls upon the free, fiery essence of Prometheus to shatter the chains that bind him—chains that represent not only literal oppression but also the illusions and false ideals (the very phantoms of glory, honor, wrath, and righteousness) that perpetuate human conflict. Should Prometheus break free, the poem envisions a profound restoration: unity among all living things, the healing of humanity's fractured relationships, and the reconnection of the earth with the wider cosmos. This closing image transforms the poem from a lament into a prayer—an urgent call for liberation not just of one suffering figure, but of all humanity, and indeed of existence itself, from the destructive cycles that 1914 so brutally exposed.

# Expanding "1914": War, Myth, and the Plea for Liberation

The poem "1914" stands as a profound meditation on the catastrophe of the First World War, using the ancient myth of Prometheus as its central organizing image. Prometheus, the Titan punished eternally for his gift of fire to humanity—chained to a rock, his liver devoured daily by an eagle only to regenerate each night for further torment—becomes a haunting metaphor for the human condition during wartime. Just as Prometheus suffers endlessly without release, so too does humanity find itself bound to a cycle of violence and anguish, tormented not by divine punishment but by its own constructed ideals.

The poem suggests that the true chains binding humanity are not literal but ideological: the seductive and destructive concepts of glory, honor, and righteousness that nations invoke to justify slaughter. These abstractions, the poem implies, function much like the eagle that perpetually wounds Prometheus—they promise meaning and nobility while actually perpetuating suffering without end. Soldiers march to their deaths believing they serve transcendent causes, yet the poem strips away this illusion to reveal the raw horror beneath: young men dying in trenches, families shattered, and a continent bleeding itself dry for concepts that offer no genuine consolation, only endless repetition of pain.

The poem's deeper power emerges in its final movement, where it transforms from lament into supplication. The closing plea represents a desperate cry for humanity to be freed from its self-imposed Promethean torment—to break free from the false ideals that chain it to perpetual violence. This is not merely a wish for the war's end, but a more radical vision: an appeal for humanity to release itself from the very concepts of glory and righteousness that make such wars thinkable and justifiable in the first place.

In its final vision, the poem reaches beyond the immediate carnage of 1914 to imagine something larger and more hopeful—a restored harmony encompassing "all living things." This closing image suggests that the war's violence has ruptured not just human relationships but the broader fabric of existence itself, the natural order that connects humanity to the earth and to other forms of life. The poem's ultimate significance, then, lies in this movement from suffering to aspiration: it does not merely document horror but reaches toward reconciliation, imagining a peaceful earth where the false idols of nationalism and militaristic honor have been abandoned, and where humanity might finally be unchained from its self-inflicted Promethean fate. This vision of restored harmony gives the poem its lasting power—transforming a specific historical catastrophe into a timeless meditation on humanity's capacity for both self-destruction and redemption.
outputs.L5:
# The Glory of Vultures

When people think of vultures, images of death and decay often come to mind—these birds are frequently maligned in folklore and popular culture, cast as omens of doom or symbols of greed. Yet this reputation does a profound disservice to one of nature's most remarkable and ecologically vital creatures.

Consider the vulture's extraordinary biological gifts. Their keen eyesight can spot a carcass from thousands of feet in the air. Their digestive systems are so acidic that they can safely consume bacteria-laden meat that would kill most other animals, including anthrax spores and botulinum toxin. In this sense, vultures are nature's sanitation workers, preventing the spread of disease by swiftly removing carrion that might otherwise fester and become breeding grounds for pathogens.

There is genuine glory in this role, even if it lacks the romance we associate with eagles or falcons. Vultures perform an essential service that keeps ecosystems healthy and balanced. Without them, the spread of diseases like rabies, anthrax, and botulism would increase dramatically, as evidenced by tragic real-world consequences. In parts of India, a catastrophic decline in vulture populations during the 1990s—caused by a veterinary drug toxic to the birds—led to a surge in feral dog populations feeding on carcasses instead. This, in turn, contributed to a rise in rabies cases among humans, illustrating just how crucial vultures are to public health.

Beyond their practical value, vultures possess a majestic quality of their own. Watching a group of vultures circle effortlessly on thermal currents, riding invisible columns of rising air with barely a wingbeat, is to witness a masterclass in aerial efficiency. Species like the Andean condor, with wingspans exceeding ten feet, embody a kind of quiet grandeur—patient, watchful, and supremely adapted to their niche.

Many cultures throughout history have recognized this, honoring vultures rather than shunning them. In ancient Egypt, the vulture was associated with the goddess Nekhbet, a protector of pharaohs. Zoroastrian traditions in Persia developed sky burial practices, entrusting the dead to vultures as a final act of returning the body to nature. These traditions understood something we often forget: that death and decay are not aberrations to be hidden away, but natural processes essential to the cycle of life, and vultures are the devoted custodians of that cycle.

Today, many vulture species face severe population declines due to poisoning, habitat loss, and human persecution. Conservation efforts are urgently needed to protect these birds—not despite their unglamorous role, but because of it. Their glory lies not in beauty alone, but in their quiet, essential work of cleansing and renewal, work that deserves far more recognition and respect than it typically receives.

To truly appreciate vultures is to embrace a different definition of majesty—one rooted in purpose, resilience, and ecological necessity rather than conventional notions of beauty or power.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem titled "1914" that uses the myth of Prometheus to comment on the horrors of war.
counterfactuals.output:
# 1914

They chained him to the rock and called it order,
the vulture sent each dawn to do its work—
Prometheus, who stole the coal of fire
and gave it to the shivering tribes of men.

We took that fire and forged it into shells.
We took that fire and learned to breathe it back
at boys who'd never asked for warmth, only
for morning, for the chance to see their hands

grow old and spotted, holding someone's child.
The gods, they say, were jealous of the flame—
but who is jealous now, watching from wherever
gods retreat to when their gifts turn feral?

In Flanders fields the fire has gone to ground,
seeping through the clay in mustard clouds,
and every man becomes his own Prometheus,
bound not to stone but to the wire, the mud,

the endless noon that never brings the dusk.
The liver grows back nightly in the wound—
this is the myth's cruel mathematics: pain
that regenerates to feed tomorrow's pain.

We built cathedrals to the god of light
and melted down the bells to make the guns.
We taught our sons the alphabet of fire
then handed them the matches, called it duty.

Somewhere the eagle circles, keeps its schedule,
finds no shortage of exposed and open chests.
The rock is Europe now. The chains are treaties.
The fire we stole still burns—we feed it well.

What Titan gave us, we have given back
transfigured: not the warmth that cooks the bread
but the blaze that swallows harvests, homes, and names,
and calls this progress, calls this a new age.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a formal, elevated sonnet-style poem about World War I, invoking classical mythology and imagery of chains, vultures, and eternal suffering.
counterfactuals.output:
# Prometheus in Flanders

Upon the crags where old Prometheus lay,
Chained fast to stone for fire stolen and given,
The vulture came each dawn to rend and flay
The endless wound that never once was riven.

So now the fields of Flanders bear the same,
Barbed wire twisted for the ancient chain,
And every soul consumed in mustard flame
Regrows by night the flesh torn twice in pain.

Old Ares walks these trenches, drunk with rust,
While Nike's wings lie broken in the clay;
The gods have turned Olympus into dust
And left us here to suffer and decay.

Eternal is the debt no man can pay—
We bleed like Titans, chained till judgment day.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Can you write a poem in the style of early 20th-century war poetry, referencing Prometheus as a symbol of humanity's endless suffering and hope for freedom?
counterfactuals.output:
# The Chained Fire

Beneath the crag where eagles wheel and cry,
He lies as he has lain ten thousand years,
His liver torn beneath the brazen sky,
Regrown each dawn to feed tomorrow's tears.
We are his children, born of stolen flame,
Marching now through mud and wire and gas—
Each war a vulture circling with his name,
Each peace a healing that will never last.

I saw a boy today who might be him,
Nailed to no rock, but to a shattered tree,
His eyes still lit with fire grown dim,
Still burning for a world he'll never see.
The generals speak of glory, speak of right,
But glory feeds on us like birds on flesh—
We gave you warmth, we gave you means of light,
And still you tear the wound and start afresh.

Yet something in the chained god will not break,
Some ember that the vultures cannot find—
Perhaps it is for hope's own bitter sake
He suffers on, defiant and half-blind.
The wire hums like a lyre in the wind,
The shells fall like the anger of dead gods,
And still we dream that somewhere men will end
This endless court where Zeus deals out the rods.

Prometheus, forgive us if we've made
Your gift a curse, your fire into this—
The trenches where our courage goes to fade,
The gas that turns our breathing into hiss.
Yet still we reach, still steal a bit of flame
From every dawn that finds us breathing yet,
And in the mud we whisper still your name,
As if the chains might one day know regret.

So let him hang between the earth and sky,
Our patron saint of suffering and light—
For if he still can hope, then so can I,
Though buried in this endless, bloody night.
The fire he gave still burns in shattered hands
That reach past wire toward some far off spring,
Where chains fall broken on forgotten lands,
And men remember what it means to sing.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a poem reflecting on the outbreak of 1914, blending themes of glory, honor, and divine punishment with the image of a chained rebel who still offers salvation.
counterfactuals.output:
**August, 1914**

The bells rang out like iron prayers
across a continent gone mad with light,
and boys who'd never held a rifle
polished brass and called it right.

They spoke of glory, spoke of honor,
words worn smooth as ancient coin,
while emperors and kings shook hands
and drew the lines that would purloin

a generation's unlived years.
The cathedrals swelled with hymns of pride,
each nation's God enlisted, blessed,
as if the sky took either side.

*This is the flood*, some prophet muttered,
watching trains pull east and west,
*the old world drowns in its own glory,
and calls the drowning its own test.*

For what is war but judgment rendered
on a species proud enough to build
such engines of its own destruction
and name the wreckage God's own will?

And somewhere, chained to rock and reason,
a rebel watched the armies pour—
the one who stole the fire once,
the one mankind keeps chaining for.

He'd given light against the mandate,
had suffered for it, bound and torn,
yet still he called down through the smoke stacks,
still he offered, still he warned:

*I gave you flame to see each other,
not to burn the fields you've sown.
I gave you voice to sing of mercy,
not this psalm of blood and bone.*

*I am the rebel they still punish,
I am the debt they'll never pay,
yet even chained I keep extending
this ruined hand—there is a way.*

But drums are louder than dead prophets,
and glory drowns the quieter creed,
so the guns of August kept on singing
their hymn of honor, want, and greed.

The chained one watched the fields turn crimson,
watched empires crown their sons with lead,
and somewhere in that human thunder
a silence held the waiting dead—

waiting still, as decades gathered,
waiting for the debt called due,
while high above the smoking rubble
a rebel's chains cut through and through,

offering still, though no one listened,
the old forbidden gift of light—
not glory's borrowed, bloodied splendor,
but something gentler. Harder. Right.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a lyrical anti-war poem that ends on a note of hope, using cosmic and mythological imagery to suggest reconciliation between mankind and the universe.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Long Reconciliation

Once, they say, the stars were forged in violence—
old suns collapsing, gods devouring gods,
and Chaos wept its children out as light.
So maybe we are only doing what
the universe first taught us: how to burn,
how to consume, how to become undone
and call it order, call it victory.

But listen—

Atlas did not choose to hold the sky.
He simply stood, one moment at a time,
beneath a weight that would have broken worlds,
because someone had to, and he was there,
and even titans learn the shape of patience.

We have made our own Atlas of the earth—
each mother lifting sons from rubbled beds,
each father teaching daughters to walk soft
across the graves that no one meant to dig,
each ordinary soul that holds the sky
one unremarkable, essential day.

The missiles trace the arcs that comets drew
a thousand years before we named the fire.
We are not new. Our grief is not original.
Even Prometheus, chained to his rock,
believed the fire he stole was worth the pain—
believed that light could be a kind of mercy,
not only ash, not only scorched-black bone.

Perhaps that's what we're owed: not absolution,
but the slow unclenching of the fist,
the way Persephone comes back each spring
not because winter loses, but because
the earth and sky agreed to share the year—
half darkness, half the green returning world.

I want to tell you war is written in us
like constellations—fixed, mythological,
unchangeable as Orion's belt.
But even stars burn out. Even the night
rearranges what it thought was permanent.
The astronomers will tell you: light we see
is often light that left its source long dead—
so let the old wars be the light we're done with,
traveling toward us only as a echo,
arriving here already in the past.

Look up. The same sky holding all our wreckage
holds also this: the patient turn of seasons,
the way that Icarus's melted wings
still teach us where the danger lies in reaching,
not that we shouldn't reach.

We are half-myth, half-mortal, half-forgiven
already, if we choose to call it so.
The universe does not require our violence
to keep its vast and burning wheels in motion.
It only asks we notice, now and then,
how light arrives from wounds already healing,
how even Atlas, in the old stories,
was promised, someday, someone else would come
and lift the sky, and let him rest, and see
what he had held so long: a world still turning,
still turning toward the morning, toward the sun.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
